h1: Returning to brewing after a career break
title: Back to Brewing After a Career Break | Craft Beer School
desc: How to get back into brewing after a career break: what has changed in the trade, what to refresh and how to explain the gap to employers.
teaser: The basics of brewing have not changed in your time away. The kit, the packaging and the hop products may have.
standfirst: Brewers step away for children, caring, health, study or a spell in another industry. Coming back is common and very doable. The work is in refreshing your hands-on skills, catching up on what has moved and telling the story of the gap with confidence.
sections:
Malt, water, hops and yeast still behave the way they did. Mash conversion still happens at roughly 62 to 72 °C. Mash pH still wants to sit around 5.2 to 5.6. Lagers still ferment cool and ales still ferment warmer. If you understood the process before your break, that knowledge is intact.

What fades is speed and confidence on the floor: reading a fermentation at a glance, judging a transfer by sound, knowing which valve sticks. Those come back with a few weeks of hands-on work. Do not let a rusty brew day convince you the knowledge has gone. It has not.

It also helps to remember why you were hired the first time. A head brewer values judgement built over years. A break of a few years does not undo that, as long as you can show you are current on the practical side.
What may have changed while you were away

Depending on how long you have been out, expect some of these:

  • Packaging: many Indian craft breweries now can beer as well as pour it, which brings canning lines, seamer checks and oxygen control.
  • Hop products: concentrated pellets, cryogenic hop products and hop extracts are more widely used, especially in hazy IPAs.
  • Styles: hazy IPAs, fruited sours and low alcohol beers are on more menus.
  • Data: more breweries log fermentations digitally and track numbers such as dissolved oxygen and brewhouse efficiency in spreadsheets or apps.

Read through two or three recent tap lists from breweries you would like to work for. That alone tells you which styles and techniques you need to be comfortable with.

If there is one technical area to brush up, make it packaging and oxygen pickup. Oxygen in finished beer causes staling and fades hop aroma quickly. Many breweries aim for dissolved oxygen below about 50 parts per billion in the package, measured with a dedicated meter. Purging cans or bottles with carbon dioxide, filling with low turbulence and capping or seaming promptly all help.

Canned beer in Indian heat is unforgiving. A can that picked up oxygen at filling and then sat in a 35 °C storeroom will taste stale within weeks. Employers know this. A returning brewer who can talk about it sensibly sounds current immediately.
Get your hands wet before you apply

Nothing replaces doing. Some practical routes back:

  • Brew at home again, keeping a full brew sheet for each batch.
  • Offer a few shifts at a local brewpub, even cleaning and cellar work.
  • Join a short course with practical sessions to rebuild the routine.
  • Volunteer at a beer festival or tasting event to rebuild your network.

A few weeks of this gives you something recent to talk about in interviews. It also rebuilds stamina. Brewery work is physical, with 25 kg malt bags and heavy kegs. Your back will remind you if you have been at a desk.

Employers mainly want to know two things: are you committed now and are your skills current? Answer both directly. One or two sentences on why you stepped away is enough. You do not owe anyone details about family or health.

Then move to what you have done to get back up to speed: the batches you have brewed, the course you took, the shifts you worked, the reading you have done on packaging or new hop products. If you worked in another industry during the break, say what you learned there. Project management, people management and data skills all transfer.
Consider adjacent roles as a way back

If a head brewer role is not open straight away, look sideways. Quality control, cellar work, packaging, sales and sensory roles all keep you close to the beer. Our guides on brewery quality control careers and brewery sales careers cover two of the most common routes. A beer sommelier path also suits brewers with strong sensory skills.

An adjacent role is not a step down if it gets you back into a brewery. Many brewers move back into production within a year once the team has seen them work.

Pick one beer style you used to brew well. Brew it again this month, at home or on borrowed kit, with a complete brew sheet: water treatment, mash temperature and pH, boil time, hop additions, original gravity, fermentation temperature and final gravity. Compare the result with your old notes if you still have them. Where the beer falls short is exactly where to focus your refresher.
faqs: Is it hard to get back into brewing after a break?
Usually not, if you refresh your practical skills and show you are current. The science has not changed. Kit, packaging and hop products may have.
How should I explain a career gap to a brewery?
Briefly and plainly. Give one or two sentences on why you stepped away, then focus on what you have done recently to get back up to speed.
What should a returning brewer learn first?
Packaging and oxygen control, especially canning. Low dissolved oxygen is central to fresh beer and many breweries now can their beer.
Are adjacent roles a good way back?
Yes. Quality control, cellar, packaging, sales and sensory roles keep you in the brewery and often lead back to production.
